record.paper_title: The Future of Primordial Black Holes: Open Questions and Roadmap
record.original_question: Can improved statistics from next-generation gravitational-wave and gravitational-microlensing experiments use the joint redshift and mass distributions of black-hole candidates to conclusively distinguish PBHs from astrophysical counterparts, despite single-event ambiguities and rare astrophysical or non-Gaussian scenarios that can mimic PBH candidates?

evidence.quote: Two of the most fundamental PBH probes that distinguish them from astrophysical counterparts are their redshift and mass distributions.This combination provides an armoury of smoking guns that will inevitably enrich the next generation of gravitational wave and gravitational microlensing experiments.

Confirmation will require improved statistics as single events may not be conclusive. it is only too easy to come up with rare events that can masquerade as PBH candidates, for example by appealing to higher order generations of merging events or to non-Gaussianity.

We have laid out a possible future road map for definitively assessing whether PBHs can present a viable candidate for dark matter, or possibly contribute to other astrophysical or even quantum cosmology anomalies.

artifact.category_tag: primordial black holes and gravitational-wave statistics
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Primordial black holes (PBHs) are hypothetical black holes formed in the early universe, as opposed to astrophysical black holes (ABHs) that arise from stellar collapse or hierarchical mergers. Two distinguishing observables are (i) the redshift distribution p_PBH(z) versus p_ABH(z) of merger or microlensing events, and (ii) the mass distribution p_PBH(m) versus p_ABH(m) of the compact-object population. Next-generation gravitational-wave detectors (e.g., Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer, LISA) and gravitational-microlensing surveys are expected to provide much larger and higher-precision catalogues of compact-object events with measured redshifts and masses.

Question: Given idealized but realistic forecasts for the joint mass–redshift event statistics achievable by such next-generation gravitational-wave and gravitational-microlensing experiments, can a statistical analysis of the joint distribution p(m, z) of black-hole candidates conclusively discriminate a PBH population from an astrophysical population, in the sense of yielding a hypothesis test whose Type-I and Type-II error rates can both be made arbitrarily small with sufficient observation time? In particular, is it possible to design such a test that remains decisive against contaminating astrophysical scenarios known to mimic PBH-like signatures—including higher-generation hierarchical mergers and rare events arising from primordial non-Gaussianity—despite the inherent ambiguity of single events?

Determine whether such a conclusive discrimination strategy exists, characterize the minimal catalogue size and measurement precision required, and identify any fundamental obstructions (degeneracies in p(m, z) between PBH and astrophysical models) that would prevent it.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a forward-looking observational/cosmological program rather than a settled theorem. Current literature (post-2024 reviews on PBH dark matter and GW forecasts) treats the question as open: joint mass–redshift distributions are widely identified as the most promising discriminator, but no conclusive observational confirmation or no-go result exists, and degeneracies with hierarchical-merger and non-Gaussian astrophysical scenarios remain under active study.

status_evidence.title: The Future of Primordial Black Holes: Open Questions and Roadmap
status_evidence.snippet: Lays out roadmap noting that confirmation will require improved statistics from next-generation GW and microlensing experiments and that single events may be inconclusive.
status_evidence.claim: The discrimination of PBHs from astrophysical counterparts via joint mass–redshift statistics is presented as an open future program.
